utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is an application by the Prosecution. Perhaps we could have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I appear today. Maybe one of my colleagues will join me in due course, I'm not sure. But I'm also assisted by Ms. Milenov who has had a great deal to do with the logging and pursuit of these applications on our behalf. And I don't know how I could have overlooked it: And Ms. Dicklich who is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Vladimir Djeric. I'm Advisor to the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Serbia and Montenegro. With me today are Mr. Sasa Obradovic, who is the Deputy Head of our International Legal Service in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, and Mr. Panceski, who is the First Secretary of the Embassy of Serbia and Montenegro at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, we have had your application, your original application of the 13th of December. We have the government's response of the 7th of February. We have your reply, 27th of February, and we have attached to that a useful document, the schedule of pending requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the colour-coded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The colour-coded document, very easy to follow, and we're grateful for that. So we have the arguments. It may be helpful if there are matters of detail you want to refer us to, and we can also perhaps limit the argument to the really relevant matters, some matters having been closed, as we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if you got an update on the schedule, but if you haven't, can I bring you up-to-date by telling you that other matters genuinely are closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the 27th of February is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And on the second sheet, in blue, RFA number 92, that is now closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning over two sheets to item 207A and B, documentation relating to the FRY investigation at Izbica. I don't know if I'm going too fast. I was getting ahead of myself this morning, I think. There is one where there's been a development, as we understand it, to this extent: That the pathologist who has done the work at Izbica is owed a very large sum of money by the government of Serbia and Montenegro, and until she's paid that money, she's not going to hand over many of the documents that relate to that crime scene. And so if that be right, the documents should be in the possession of the government, but by not paying her bill, they find themselves in the position of not being able to answer our proper request. And the Chamber will see the clear significance of material in relation to Izbica for the Kosovo indictment. The next page, or continuation of the same page of the last part of this, I'm not sure which, but at number 249, we, I think, record that some documentation has been received and there's a balance outstanding. There is some uncertainty. We have not been able to resolve that uncertainty by today. It may be that we have received the outstanding material and, therefore, we must suspend our position in relation to that one. And the same problem arises, of uncertainty, in relation to 279, over the page, request for Republic of Serbia Assembly documentation. We may have received this material pursuant to different numbered RFAs, numbers 311 and 203. And so, obviously, we should suspend our position in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you are inviting me or allowing me to make a short opening statement to clarify the issues, I really say very little but the following: This application, of course, relates to specific documents but has been used by the government authorities as a way of raising for the first time the issue of access to archives, and you'll find, I think it's in paragraph 9 of their document - I'll just check that - they say, I think, "As a sign of goodwill and despite its general position vis-a-vis the right of access to archives, it's proposed that expert meetings be held to discuss modalities." Well, applications for access to and documents from archives have been being made for whatever it is, a year or 18 months, before that response was filed. And although there may from time to time have been requests for more specificity, it had never been suggested that in some way archives were off limits, and that would be an astonishing proposition to make, for the Chamber may think that cooperation of the type required of states really falls into three potential levels. At the top you could have - and there is absolutely no reason why you should not have - states actively searching their archives and documents to find the materials that they would know better than we ever could would assist this Chamber in bringing these proceedings to a proper, secure, and well-informed conclusion. And indeed if it be the case, as we have reason to believe it may be, that the documentary archives exist in various places and are certainly complete in relation to some if not all of these three indictments, the Chamber may well ask itself just how short these proceedings could have been if a proactive - to use a word I don't particularly like but nevertheless has a meaning - had taken a proactive stance in relation to this trial and had searched its materials to find what would have dealt with the issues in this case. Well, we must bear in mind that cooperation does not mean that. The next level of cooperation which has been manifested in relation to archives by Croatia, the Federation, and the RS, is to permit access to archives for survey purposes and thereafter for specific request purposes which make the doing of the job of the OTP that much easier and more certain of safe, secure, reliable, well-founded success. And success is judged by getting the right answer, not just by getting some answer. Now, it happened that the government represented here today did, for a time, allow that to happen. Over a year or so ago in relation to, I think, the archives of the Ministry of Justice. And so when they say there's a rule against it, it's a rule that either they've forgotten, overlooked or is only of recent creation. But what we know is that this government and in relation to this case is not adopting the attitude that other parts of the former Yugoslavia have adopted. It was slow coming sometimes. Your Honour in particular will remember the position of the authorities in the Bosnian Croat cases and the timing of the opening of their archives brought problems but eventually it came. Well, that's not the level of cooperation we're getting here. The level of cooperation we're getting here is this: If we can identify a document with sufficient clarity that its existence is not or cannot be denied, and if we persist in the application, we get them, or we may get them. But this has to be said when it's being asserted by the government, not just in this court, that they have been cooperative, there is a great deal of a difference between quality and quantity. And it may not harm the government concerned to provide a quantity of materials if they actually retain the documents that are of particular significance. If Your Honour will be good enough to go in the colour-coded document to one example and then I'll provide you with another document, to look at 219, which is to be found, I think, about the third, fourth sheet. This is now the 25th of June outstanding. A hundred and twenty documents, all narrowly focused relating to the testimony of a protected witness, as he then was, the witness in respect of whom there is the outstanding problem over the provision of a waiver that will enable him to come here. You'll see the limited response that we got. Some documents received on the 8th and 30th of August. Cannot provide four, 90 pending. Now, we do not accept that there is not a connection, a connection reflecting, I'm afraid, a determination to keep us from presenting these materials in the attitude towards this particular request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a statement -- let me interrupt you on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's statement here that some of the documentation was destroyed in the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think if I'm right, the statement is somewhat more circumspect than that, and I think it says "may have been." The Chamber may -- I'm not sure if you've had evidence of this, but there were in place at the time of the NATO bombing, regulations on the storage and I think duplication of materials to avoid their loss in times of trouble or war, and there is absolutely no reason to believe other than that these documents, most of them, would have been -- and you're quite right, there is a statement -- a letter dated the 30th, received on the 31st of January, coming from the Deputy Minister Nenad Milic, speaking of Kosovo, and VJ documents and other, saying that they do not have the requested documents. But again, that doesn't reflect the existence of copies. And we do not accept that these documents would have existed in a single copy and that all those, if any have been, would have been the subject of destruction in the NATO bombing. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice when, it says in the column that the FRY government has stated that it cannot provide four documents, what does that mean, that it is not able to or it is not obliged to or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that Mr. Djeric will be able in due course to help us further with that. I'll look up the terminology as it came to us. But I should also say this at this stage, because I think it's important. And if Mr. Djeric wishes us to go into closed session, I shall quite understand. There has been given at one or other stages of negotiations another reason why documentation may not be produced, and that reason has also, I think, been given or obliquely referred to at times when it's been suggested to me that I should be prepared to put my name to an application for blanket closed-session testimony for documentation, which I'm plainly not prepared to do. Not only am I not prepared to do it, it would be pretty useless if I did that. I can imagine the response of the Chamber if I said we want to put all this documentation in for some category reason closed session. The Chamber would very smartly tell me that it was nothing to do with that, and we could make an application and if it was individually supportable document-by-document you might review it. There's been another underlying reason for the authorities' concern about the publicity that will be given to this documentation. As I say, if Mr. Djeric, who will inevitably know what I'm referring to, would prefer me to mention this in closed session, I will. Otherwise, I'll mention it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, if you follow the point, would you wish us to go into -- it to be a private session, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't know, Your Honour, whether it would be appropriate that we give some general comments first, because the Prosecution filed its reply in which it raised certain new points, and of course we will be happy to answer specific points in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us, from an abundance of caution, let us go into private session since we don't know what the point is. We'll go into private session briefly

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this colour-coded document, which I've now been able to update a little bit, of course deals with requests each of which cover many documents. It seems to me it might be helpful for you to have just a snapshot of, say, the first roughly 150 documents. Not rough, the first. The most important, the most valuable 150 documents. We have prepared a little list that are extracted from these. May I just make that available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What would be helpful from my point of view would be a list of what's outstanding. No need to produce it now. I can work it out from your code, which gives it to us, but what I would like to hear about is what is outstanding now and what is the most valuable. It may be that this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is one way of dealing with it, yes. If you'd be good enough, please, then to look at this, which is priority list. And I'm not going to ask you to go through, I think it's 162 documents, but I can ask you to have a look at a few of them. 162, yes. Just to see both the age of the request and the obvious significance of the document. You can see, of course, on sheet 1 that these requests go back to April of 2001. If you'd be good to turn to page 2, item 8 at the top of the page, requested in August 2001, re-requested under the most -- perhaps the most significant RFA, number 219, the one I've just referred to before we went into closed session, Supreme Defence Council minutes of meetings from the 27th of April of 1992 to the 5th of October, 2000. Interestingly enough, we've been provided with a few from 1992 and 1998, but nothing from that intervening period. Number 9 is the same topic but this time stenographic notes. Another example, number 15. The Chamber will recall the limited amount of written material, printed material, so far available to it in respect to the Supreme Command for Kosovo. Requested on the 15th of August, an inadequate response received on the 26th of December, 2002, pending for over a year since then. If we turn over the page to number 19, that appears to be a request dated the 16th of October of 2002. In fact, that was itself a follow-up to a request made on the 15th of August, 2001. Significance, absolutely obvious: Commands, orders, directives, instructions and orders for security of combat operations for other activities, plans, notifications, reports. Right. I must slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you'd just go back to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The inadequate response to the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll dig out the response for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just let me know in what way was it inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I'm on -- the response that we assert was inadequate said this: "In order to acquire the requested information, this ministry addressed the Yugoslav Army General Staff Commission for Cooperation at The Hague Tribunal which notified us by a note dated the 2nd of October, 2002, that the requested documentation was not under the jurisdiction of the Federal Ministry of Defence and the Yugoslav army. This ministry then turned to the military cabinet of the FRY president, which by a note of the 21st of October informed us that the military cabinet and other offices of the FRY president didn't possess documents related to the Supreme Command, nor are provisions on the Supreme Command to be found in the constitution, law of defence, or law of the Yugoslav army." Now, we know that to be incorrect. We have since then had possession of some Supreme Command documents which I think have been provided I think through -- one or two through Vasiljevic and possibly one, I think -- one or more through Rade Markovic. But this is a small tip of the iceberg. The documents exist, and this is rather like the game of Cups or whatever they call it in America. This one doesn't have it, that one doesn't have it, and they don't exist. It's a question of finding where they are. And we say that's an inadequate response. And it's a very important piece of information, because as the Chamber will well understand in Kosovo, central to determination of that part of this case is how the operations were conducted and who was ultimately giving the orders and when plans were formed. The Supreme Command will provide us the answer to that, we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These -- so I have the position, these 150 documents are outstanding today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is only, as it were, the best 150 or, viewed from another perspective, maybe the worst. And I was at number 19, reviewing why its relevance for the Kosovo part of the indictment was so obvious. I think I've really dealt with it. The last three lines. I've dealt with it. One can see its absolute essential relevance to the case. Another perhaps relevant document, just again to select one, would be number 27, a specific request for orders and instructions issued by the Joint Command for Kosovo between the 1st of November 1998 and the 19th of June 1999, to which we received a response in July of last year stating that these documents may have been housed in a building that was destroyed by NATO. That's where the word "may" appears, a response that we, respectfully, find insufficient. If the Chamber would then turn over to sheet 5. We're now in an extensive request, 174A, which is itself a repeat or a refinement of 174, which is issued in April 2002. So the immediate 174A of October 2002. Correspondence between the Joint Command and the MUP staff for Kosovo, the Joint Command and the 3rd Army, the Joint Command and the Pristina Corps. The inadequate response I'll just read to you. The response is as follows: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was formed on the order of the president in June 1998 without any specific document. The command operated until October of that year, following which unofficial meetings were held where the current security situation was analysed. According to the military organs' knowledge, the documents from the joint command for Kosovo and Metohija related to military issues were delivered to the incumbent chief of the cabinet of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's president on termination of its work late in 1998. The buildings where these documents may have been housed were demolished and destroyed during NATO aggression."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't question that one, Mr. Nice, because it states definitively that the building was destroyed, but you question when it says the documents may have been housed in a building that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. We question it on that basis. And, Your Honour, it's well for us all to remember this is a former communist state, as people have explained to us, where documentation and recording of things was an absolute routine. We do not accept that important documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of this kind existed in one copy only and were then stored in one copy only. We say that is just unrealistic. Oh, yes. I'm grateful to Ms. Milenov because I see I signed the document, so I made the request. We requested of them detail of this "may have been housed" assertion, and I think got nothing. Got this much -- got nothing, I'm afraid. Just an acknowledgement of the letter. But, Your Honour, this is all, in a sense, if we go on from where we are on page 5, to go to page 6 and to items 48 and 49. We now come to request for assistance number 219. And of course the colour-coded document doesn't necessarily reflect the quantity of materials or the weight of significance of materials underlying any particular request for assistance. 48 was a request in May of 2002 followed up on September for minutes of the session of the council for coordination of positions on state policy. And then 219, number 49, picks up with a request for stenographic recordings of these meetings, it being our understanding that such stenographic recordings were made. And you'll now see, over the next four sheets, documents for 219, and I just pick up four of them, I think, or five of them. 51, at the bottom of the page, training of volunteers from outside Serbia by special units of the VJ. Over the page. Reports on the cooperation of the Serbian RDB and the VJ in Eastern Slavonia. That's number 52. Number 55, report of the 26th of November 1995 on an award ceremony for members of a unit of anti-terrorist action. These are all quite specific documents, so that even at the low level of cooperation that we say is all that's reflected by the government's approach, there's all the specificity there that's wanted. At the foot, 58, VJ KOS reports on the work of the JSA of 1996. Over the page to page 8, number 62, reports on meetings of Bosnian SDS to discuss conflicts between Karadzic and Mladic, and so on. And, Your Honour, we could go on, but I think that I've taken some time. There are many -- well, 219 just goes on and on. And these specific documents -- for example, look at number 87. An order from Perisic dated the 10th of November, 1993 - fully identified - concerning the creation of the 30th and 40th personnel centres, the significance of which will not be lost on Your Honours, I have no doubt. Or documents further up the page, 76 and 77, which would deal with the accused's direct control of the VS. Over the page to page 11, number 88. Still in the same request for assistance, 219. A letter of the 29th of September, 1995, from Colonel Sinisa Perisic, addressed to the military cabinet of the president of the FRY concerning training of volunteers. Or the next document, 89, response of the military cabinet of the president of the FRY to that letter. Your Honour, we would invite this Chamber to exercise its powers, and it's not just 54(A), it's 54 and all its other powers, and in recognition of the real burden that is on the Chamber, that is on the Office of the Prosecutor to get this case dealt with securely and within a reasonable time, to order the production of these documents. And if I may put it in the vernacular, to have nothing to do with this assertion that in some way archives are off limits. They weren't off limits for Croatia, they weren't off limits for the Federation, they weren't off limits for the RS, and they weren't off limits for this government until they received our application, and they suddenly said that they were. We can't do our job and we can't discharge our duty to the international community without documents. Well, we can; it just takes a lot longer and is a lot harder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asking us, therefore, to make an order, are you, today, compelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when you've reflected on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, whenever. But that's what you're asking us to do, compelling the production of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what about the answer "may have been destroyed in the NATO bombing" or "destroyed in NATO bombing"? What do we do about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They haven't made that answer yet. It's always been surrounded by a "may have" and it says nothing of copies. And this is a government that knows it has to cooperate and that should be held to account. And in our submission, if they choose to say at any stage absolutely every copy of a document has been destroyed, that may be one thing. They haven't said it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They have -- on one occasion they did say that the building was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The building was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In which documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May have been kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That may have been kept or were in fact kept?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because I think you want to be careful, Mr. Nice, about questioning the bona fides of a government, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply reading the material as it comes to me very cautiously, and aware of the existence of copies. But I'll just look up that one and come back to it to make that Your Honour is right in that characterisation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. There's a point we want clarified because it's not clear to the members of the Trial Chamber. Are you asking for access to the archives in the sense of going to the archives and carrying out your own searches, or are you asking for the archives to be handed over to you completely or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're certainly not asking for the archives to be handed over. We are asking to be provided with access to the archives sufficient for us to do our work which involves, of course, a staged level of access in exactly the same way as it operated -- or very similar to the way it operated with the other entities, namely, access to the indices, survey of the archive first and then have access to the documents when you've had that approach. Sensible way to deal with it. We certainly don't want the archives handed over, no. And, Your Honour, I am reminded that it's perhaps worth my reading to you what we said in terms in relation to the destroyed archive and to which we received no response. "Further to your --" this is what I said in a letter of the -- I've forgotten the date. Thanks very much. 17th of October last year. "Further to your response of the 12th of July in which you state that the buildings in which the 1998 Joint Command documents may have been housed were destroyed by NATO, we would like to know the names of the archives, the names of the custodians responsible for the archives and documents, where those documents were located, the addresses for Joint Command documents --" sorry, "the addressees for Joint Command documents, more precise details on how and when the facility containing the documents was destroyed, log entries or other documentation showing the transfer of the 1998 Joint Command documents, and why you introduced uncertainty into the destruction of the documents by using the term 'may' as in 'may have been housed' in referring to the building that was bombed by NATO." And no response to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Okay, there is a lot of material to cover here today. Mr. Nice had about 40 minutes. Let me just begin with the -- with stressing at the outset that the government of Serbia and Montenegro is committed to meet fully its obligation under the Statute and to provide all the assistance needed to the International Tribunal. There is a strong political will of the authorities in Serbia and Montenegro to cooperate, and it is this will that has crushed the indolence of bureaucracy and resistance from various quarters in order to effect the cooperation. And the will to cooperate is evident from the information about cooperation that we submitted to the Chamber in our written response. What is also evident is that requests for assistance arrive daily and that cooperation is a process and that these requests for assistance are quite big and contain, in fact, requests for assistance for hundreds of documents. We are glad that we have maintained this level of cooperation despite significant changes in the structure of our state due to the establishment of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro. However, the present application of the Prosecution seeks to obtain something which we feel the Prosecution does not have under the Statute and Rules of this Court, and that is an unlimited right to access and survey state archives in Serbia and Montenegro. Therefore, we are glad to come before the Trial Chamber in order to have a legal determination about the extent of our obligation under -- obligations under the Statute, because it is the Court that should pronounce on this issue and not the Prosecution. And we are, of course, going to fully comply with the Court decisions. Your Honours, I would like now to address some of the contentions made by the Prosecution in their reply, if I may, and then I will turn to specific requests for assistance. Your Honours must have been puzzled, as we all are, by Prosecution's submissions in the reply. It is not really clear what the Prosecution want in its final submissions. First, in paragraph 17 of the reply, and that is at the very end of the reply, the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 54 bis, requests to have, and I'm quoting: "... a hearing with officials of Serbia and Montenegro to discuss the lack of Serbian and Montenegrin official cooperation." At the time the reply was filed, today's hearing had been long scheduled. The question then is: Does the Prosecution request one more hearing in addition to the present one? And furthermore, Rule 54 bis does not envisage a hearing to discuss the lack of cooperation. What Rule 54 bis envisages is a hearing about the application for an order to produce identifiable documents. Secondly, in the same paragraph 17 of the reply, the Prosecution requests, pursuant to Rules 39 and 54, that the Trial Chamber order Serbia and Montenegro, and I'm quoting now, "to comply with the RFAs described in the attached annex." The question here is again: What does the Prosecution really want? Are we in a proceeding under Rule 54 bis, or are we in a proceeding under Rules 39 and 54? Another question is whether this submission of the Prosecution is appropriate at this late stage of the present proceedings, considering that the application filed on 13 December 2000 did not rely at all on Rule 39. Two and a half months after the application, the Prosecution decided that it wished to rely on Rule 39. We respectfully submit to the Trial Chamber that it should refuse to consider the reply in this part. Your Honours, notwithstanding our position that the Chamber should refuse to consider Rule 39 in these proceedings, I would still like to respond to the arguments in the Prosecution's reply about the applicability of this provision. The provision of documents by states, as is well known, is governed by Rule 54 bis. Therefore, Rule 39 does not apply in this field. As far as Rule 54 is concerned, it provides for a general power of a Judge or a Trial Chamber to conduct the proceedings or conduct the investigation. With regard to the production of documents by states, this general power has been regulated in detail and exhaustively by Rule 54 bis. And this is appropriate considering the specificity of cooperation involving sovereign states and their interests. Furthermore, how could an implied power of the Chamber to issue search warrants under Rules 39 and 54 override the explicit and carefully formulated power to order production of documents under Rule 54 bis? As is well known, Rule 54 bis was a consequence of the Appeals Chamber decision in Blaskic in 1997, and it is true that before the adoption of Rule 54 bis, orders under Rule 54 were used to facilitate cooperation by states in production of documents. But even then, the Appeals Chamber carefully developed the requirements for such a cooperation and for such orders, and the said requirements were subsequently incorporated in Rule 54 bis. Therefore, we submit that first it had been the intention of the International Tribunal to exclusively and exhaustively regulate cooperation of states with regard to documents by Rule 54 bis as lex specialis. As was said in an order of the Trial Chamber in Kordic and Cerkez, dated 4th August, 2000, and I'm quoting: "Requests for order under Rule 54 of the Rules for states to produce documents and information are now -" and I repeat now - "governed by Rule 54 bis of the Rules." End of quote. That's the order for the production of documents by the European Community. Similarly, the Scheduling Order in the present case said, and I'm quoting: "Applications for orders directed to states are governed by Rule 54 bis." End of quote. Second point: Even if Rule 54 had been directly applicable in this field, this could have been possible only if orders issued would follow the requirements set by the Appeals Chamber in Blaskic, and this in turn would mean that the Prosecution would in fact have to comply with the same requirements as in Rule 54 bis. And as we demonstrated in our written response, the requests for access to archives fall outside the scope of Rule 54 bis, or in the alternative, they manifestly fail to meet its requirements as well as the requirements set by the Blaskic judgement. In addition, if Rule 39 would apply with respect to states' cooperation in respect to production of documents, this would effectively annul Rule 54, this, and would render it meaningless. First, the Prosecution could circumvent the requirements set in paragraph (A) of Rule 54 bis, especially as regards the specificity of the documents requested. Second, if production of documents by states were to be governed by Rule 39, the carefully tailored procedure for the protection of state interests in Rule 54 bis would be rendered meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to just go back to the point that you made that the requests for access to archives fall outside the scope of Rule 54 bis. Could you elaborate on that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Explain exactly why you take that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: We have elaborated in part in our written response. Our basic position is that access and survey of state archives, as requested by the Prosecution, is actually a physical access to archives, and Rule 54 bis is only regulating production of documents by states. The states are supposed to produce documents and not to allow physical access by the Prosecution to the archives. That's -- that's the first point. And as is well known, it is primarily on states to effect the cooperation. That was said in the Blaskic appeal decision. And only in very exceptional circumstances and in relation to on-site investigations and not to the access to certain documentation that the Prosecution could act independently of state organs. And we submit that we do not have such an exceptional situation. I believe that this exceptional situation was related in the Blaskic appeals decision to the cases when the authorities concerned were involved in the -- in committing the crimes or were preventing the cooperation, and we feel that, since October 2000, we have a clear difference between -- in the policy of the government with this significant change of October 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So they could get access but not by Rule 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If they could get access to the archives, it cannot be by Rule 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: They cannot. We submit that there is no right to access generally under the Statute, to access to archives except in very exceptional situations. But under Rule 54 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Suppose they were to ask for a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: That's the point that I was just about to make. We think that Rule 54 bis is lex specialis and that it exhaustively regulates this field and the search warrant cannot be, under Rule 39, directed against the state archives because it would definitely mean that one state authority searching another state authority, which is highly paradoxical in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as I said, Rule 54 bis exhaustively regulates this area. And contrary to what the Prosecution contends in its reply with regard to the production of documents by states, the Rules are neither vague nor provide only examples of actions that may be taken. True, the Rules have been subject to frequent amendments, but this does not take away their legal force and the clarity, clarity of Rule 54 bis. And as the Rules now stand, we submit the Prosecution must fulfill the requirements set forth in 54 bis. And we think that in relation to general access to archives, and that is the requests which are, I believe, in Part I of the annex to the application in these proceedings, so in relation to these requests for assistance, the Prosecution cannot possibly meet the requirements of Rule 54 bis. Now, I will now go to a point that was made in the reply but also by Mr. Nice today as illustration of the alleged authority to have access and to survey state archives. The Prosecution invokes example from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and today Croatia was mentioned. But this is done without much detail and without crucial information about these searches, such as who conducted the search, what was its scope, and pursuant to what kind of authority, whether an order or a search warrant, if any, these searches were conducted. So we are not in a position to comment these examples, but we would like to make two general observations. First, these examples concern only one state, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and no other state either in the former Yugoslavia or elsewhere. Second, this state, Bosnia-Herzegovina, has a unique constitutional structure under the Dayton-Paris peace accords, and there a large civil and military presence, international presence, has quite significant legislative, law enforcement, and executive powers. However, the Chamber will recall that the Chamber in the Simic case on 18 October 2000 issued an order to the SFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina to produce documents pursuant to Rule 54 bis and not pursuant to Rule 39 and 54. And in conclusion, we respectfully submit that the Prosecution's contention that Rule 39 is applicable should be rejected. We also submit that the Prosecution cannot meet the requirements contained in Rule 54 bis. Now I will go to the requests for assistance contained in the application, if the Chamber allows. And I'm not going to repeat what we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already said in our response. I would like to summarise and then, if there are specific questions, then we could turn to Mr. Obradovic who will have specific information about them. I have already said in response to your question, Your Honours, with regard to access to archives, the application is outside Rule 54 bis, or in the alternative, manifestly fails to meet the requirements set forth therein. The Prosecution now contends, and today as well, and I'm quoting: "The OTP has never demanded general access to archives but has sought to survey archives in order to establish what document, if any, may be pertinent to Tribunal proceedings." That's in the reply, paragraph 3. Honestly, Your Honours, we fail to see any difference. The quote, the sentence is a description of what the Judges of this Tribunal have rightfully called a fishing expedition. What the Prosecution wants is to survey the archives. What is it other but access, physical access? Then the Prosecution wants to establish what documents may be pertinent to Tribunal proceedings. What is it else than access to all documents contained in a particular archive? And that's nothing else but fishing for documents. And we respectfully submit that the Chamber should refuse to entertain such a request. Now with regard to 32 requests for assistance contained in Annex II to the application. We have demonstrated in our written response that the great majority of these requests have been responded to. However, we think that five of them can be subsumed under general access to archives as well or, in the alternative, could be -- should be regarded as too general. And I'm going to go, in a moment, into detail of these five requests. For the remaining requests, the current situation, according to our data is as follows: We responded to 18, partially have been -- I'm sorry. Six have been partially responded, and only five are still in process and have received no response at all. As the Appeals Chamber said in the Blaskic case, the Tribunal should reserve its mandatory powers only as a matter of last resort, to cases when this is really necessary. We submit that the application is premature and not necessary. Of course, should the Chamber see fit, we could go request by request. At the very end, Your Honours, I would like to say that we respectfully submit that the application should be rejected, but I would also like to reiterate the willingness of Serbia and Montenegro to cooperate with the International Tribunal not only as a matter of international legal obligation that we have but also as a matter of moral obligation, compelling us all to search for the truth and to bring to justice those responsible for horrible crimes committed on the territory of former Yugoslavia. And now if I may, I could go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why would you say the application is premature when in some cases the requests have been pending for over a year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to see exactly which requests are these. Some of the requests that have been pending for quite long, admittedly, are requests for general access to archives, requests that we feel are general access to archives. Some requests are really huge, such as request 219, and the period of time of, I believe, eight months since the -- the request number 219 was transmitted to us has allowed us to respond to certain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to find out if you have this document that we have, the priority list of documents requested. It's a document from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I consider it important for you to identify in this list those requests that relate to archives so that we can separate those from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. We have first the requests that are straightforward requests for access to archives. Do you wish me to also identify these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Are you reading from a document that you now have or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying now to get -- get it in order. Just a second. I'm sorry. Just a second. Okay. Now, I don't think that what we regard as plain access to archives requests are really here, but I will for the record just repeat. These are requests number 76, and 95, and 106. And they are --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: And 106. They're not on the priority list submitted by the Prosecution today, but they are part 1 of the Annex to the original application submitted by the Prosecution. Now, going to the requests that we feel are actually nothing else but requests for general access to archives or, in the alternative, are way too general, the first would be request number 110, which is number 7 in your -- in your table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is archival.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, we consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: And I will quote the relevant part of the request so the Chamber would immediately know what its content is. I'm quoting: "Copies of all orders issued by Colonel General Nebojsa Pavkovic or those orders issued on his behalf by the staff of the 3rd Army concerning the engagement or use of the VJ, Yugoslav army, and Serbian police forces in combat operation during the 1999 conflict in Kosovo." First point here, if I may explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: You want me to go request by request. So first point is this: We feel that this request is over-broad, because it relates not only to actions related to civilians and combatants on the ground that might have involved violations of humanitarian law but also relates to orders concerning all actions of Yugoslav forces, including those related to NATO during the bombing. That time was the time of the NATO intervention and bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this request would actually mean that we will have to hand over all the orders related to that -- to that conflict and not all the orders related to the actual actions on the ground which might have involved violations of international law. So the content and subject matter of the documents requested must be in some ways indicated here. And furthermore, this requires -- request involves hundreds of documents. So it's too burdensome without further specification, of course. If I may go further. The request number 117, which is in your table at point 10 to 12. Page 2, points 10 to 12. This request is a clear example of a general over-broad request. It relates to a period of almost ten years; from April 1992 to 5th October 2000. Not only that, it relates to the documentation of the Supreme Defence Council, which is the Commander-in-Chief of the Yugoslav armed forces. And the request includes, I'm quoting: "Laws, conclusions, decisions, orders, reports, other communications, minutes, stenographic notes of minutes of meetings," all that for a period of almost ten years. So it's way too over-broad, in our view, and it is actually a request for the archive of the Supreme Defence Council, nothing else. Or at least 90 per cent of this -- of this archive. So it's too broad in terms of its subject matter, in terms of time period, and in terms of events and places it covers, because it's not focused on the -- neither on the possible violations of the laws of war. It's not focused neither on events that are mentioned in the indictment, events in Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're saying, firstly, it is essentially a request for archival material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which, in your submission, does not fall under 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: 54 bis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And even if it did fall under 54, you contend that it is -- it is too general.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is too general, and it will be too burdensome. So it will not meet the two requirements of Rule 54 bis, paragraph (A). Now, of course, as I said, these documents involve matters completely unrelated to the proceedings. And another point is that the burden of this request is not only related to a number of documents but must also be seen in relation to the sensitivity of documents, because the burden should not be taken only as a number but also a sensitivity of documents. And finally, of course, these are highly sensitive information involving our Commander-in-Chief, and it is hard to imagine that any state would disclose this information, at least not unless and until very strict protective measures are determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that must be your practical reason for not allowing the OTP's access to the archive. I think I understand your point that -- your point is that access to archive is not possible under the regime of Rule 90 -- I'm sorry, excuse me, 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether it's possible in practical terms, whether there's some specific reason why there is some consensual under the goodwill arrangement made possible to allow them to make a search.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: As you said first, Your Honour, it's a point of law and point of principle. Second, it is obviously related to national security. And third, you mentioned whether it could be subject to some arrangement. Yes, perhaps. I'm not authorised to say that it could, but I can say that we, in vain, tried to find a modality with the Prosecution in order to meet their demands and in order to meet our concerns. And I wish to stress here that we never proposed that documents be withheld from this Trial Chamber. What we proposed only is that certain protective measures be adopted. However, in relation to -- generally to the access to archives and in relation to these other requests, we had, I have to say, trouble in receiving a workable proposal by the Prosecution. We proposed first meetings. That's mentioned in our written response. These meetings were held. Mr. Nice was in Belgrade. That was the beginning of November 2002. But after these -- and these meetings, I'm sorry, involved the heads or staff of all the relevant archives in Serbia and the federal ones. Now, after these meetings, what we received in a couple of weeks was -- were the requests which were completely the same as the ones that we received before. Only now, I believe a couple of weeks ago, we received a proposal from the Prosecution that we immediately put into a consultation process within our government, and we are hoping to have an answer rather soon. But I have to say that we have waited for such a proposal for months, if not a year. So we are very open to consultations with the Prosecution, but we can get the response from the Prosecution only after months and only with a lot of effort. And what happens sometimes, as we mentioned in our written response, is that we have a confidential content of our negotiations made public, as the Prosecution did in the application. And it's not right to say, as the Prosecution says, that we wanted to withhold the content of our consultations with them from the Trial Chamber. That's not the point. The point is that it's the usual rule of negotiations in diplomatic practice that the content of the negotiations is not made public. And the whole matter could have been resolved only if the Prosecution filed its application confidentially. But that's -- that's another story related to this process of consultations that we have with the Prosecution which we are not satisfied with, I have to say, but we hope to have progress on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this: Suppose that we were not inclined - and I'm just speaking for myself and I'm merely thinking aloud - supposing we were not inclined to make any orders today but accept your assurance that you were in good faith pursuing such documents as you think you can produce, how long do you think it would take to produce the documents, such documents as you can, on this -- the latest document, this latest extract we have, said to be the priority list? How long would you want to access that and to see whether you can produce these and produce what you would?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only talk hypothetically, of course. We have now sort of reorganisation of our government, so that would take some time. Not -- I'm talking about perhaps months or several weeks, rather. But we, in any case, feel that this application is unnecessary, because I personally signed a lot of responses to the Prosecution every day, and there are a lot of them, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. They've now come to us and asked us to do something about it. So we are under an obligation to consider it. As I say, it's a possibility. One possibility is to say, well, we would adjourn the application or we would take no action providing efforts are made, for some months, for you to make further efforts to access such documents as you can. That's what I'm inquiring, as to what sort of time you would ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djeric. We interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long would you be asking for to deal with the other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: I could say weeks, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: -- up to a month and a half. But there is one more thing, and that is there are different requests here. Some of the requests plainly cannot be fulfilled by Serbia and Montenegro. You have yourself discussed this response that the documentations may -- the documentation may have been destroyed. But there are other documents requested that plainly are not in the archives, or plainly do not exist after good faith searches that were conducted by our authorities. So I cannot commit in respect to those documents. I also cannot really commit in respect to the access to archives, and not because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's matter which we're going to consider, this point about the archives. We're not persuaded, I can tell you at the moment, that they should have access to the archives, but it's the other documents which you can produce which we are concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we -- Your Honours, if we go to these requests that we consider are subsumed to the general access to archives that I started to discuss, you will see that -- I think that in respect to them, we could -- we could have consultations with the Prosecution. You also have to consider, when taking your position, that some of these requests, such as request 309, which is in your table at the very end, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, at page 15. This request was actually sent to Serbia and Montenegro only on 6 November 2000 [sic], and so the application could not wait five weeks. And the Prosecution could not wait even five weeks and included this one in the application. I'm sorry, 6 November 2002. So this is request 309 at page 15. That's number 144 -- 143, 144, 145, 146. It's plainly no reasonable steps have been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Well -- so that was request 309. Then request 119/B and /C, which is in your table at page 2 and 3, point 17 to 23. These requests are, for instance, also quite new. They were sent only, I believe, in October, 16 of October, 2002. So we also had maybe two or three months -- three months before the application to process these requests. And as you see, they cover almost everything in a six-month period, for six months of 1999 and relate to all possible orders, directives, instructions, plans, notifications, reports, decisions, et cetera, et cetera, of all the units involved in the Kosovo conflict. And this is also something that we consider over-broad. Also we consider it quite burdensome. And finally, we consider that no reasonable steps have been taken. It is very interesting to know that request 119/C refers to war diaries, operation logs, incoming and outgoing message logs from the General Staff of Yugoslav army, et cetera. It's a very similar request to the one that needed further specification in Kordic and Cerkez Chamber order in relation to the Defence request to the Netherlands. That order was dated 27th January 2000, and then the Chamber said that the party should further specify its requests, and I'm quoting, "... for contemporaneous diaries, journals, et cetera, kept by Dutch army or intelligence personnel." This is quite similar what the Prosecution is asking from us now. I would also wish to mention request number 118, which is another request that we consider amounts to a general request for access to archives. That is points 13 to 16 at page 2 of your document. Also, it's way too broad in terms of subject matter, in terms of events and places it covers. It is also a request related to Kosovo conflict which involved, of course, bombing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we don't see how all these documents can be related to the proceedings. It furthermore involves thousands of documents, and basically the whole archives of the Supreme Command for that period. And it involves highly sensitive information for which we might have national security concerns. Now coming to request number 174, and that is the request at points 25 to basically point 42. That is pages 4, 5, and 6 of your document. We have a report that this documentation was destroyed during the bombing. I really cannot accept the contentions of the Prosecution that there is a reason not to believe the government when the government produces an information that something does not exist or has been destroyed. You will see a similar situation in respect to the request number 219. And I am again inviting you to consider the last couple of years in Serbia whereas we had a complete change of government in October 2000, and many of the documents just were not found after the change. And as the Prosecution well knows, many of the documents might -- may be found in private hands of private individuals. Also, in some cases, archives documents, records, were not kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just have a point clarified about your contention in relation to archival material. You make the point that the Prosecution has no right to access archival material, no right to physical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. access to archival material under 54 bis, and I understand that argument. But on the other hand, when you go through the list, you point to some request that you say essentially relate to archival material. So I gather the Prosecution is not requesting physical access to that material, but in your assessment the material is archival. But it doesn't seem to me that logically you can make the same argument, because all they're requesting there is that you provide documents or information from that material, even though you may wish to characterise it as archival. They're not requesting physical access to it. On that score, you'd have to confine yourself to the general objections based on the Blaskic decision, the burdensome nature, and the others that you have cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'm trying to, when I go request by request, basically to give objections in relation to the criteria that were in the Blaskic decision and 54 bis. But the point about the archives is sort of a preliminary point. One thing is to request physical access to archives, and that is what the Prosecution does in respect to certain requests for assistance. Another point is that the Prosecution, in some cases, wishes to have basically all the documents in a particular archive, and that is nothing else for us than the access to archives. If the Prosecution wishes to have all the documents of the Supreme Defence Council for the period of 1999 up to 2000, including stenographic notes, decisions, orders, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, that is nothing else. What is then, in other words, left in the archive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the proper basis, following Blaskic, is that the request is too general and broad, not that it is archival.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: It is indeed. Yes. Yes. Indeed it is also general and too broad, and in the alternative, we argue that these requests do not fulfill the Blaskic criteria and do not fulfill Rule 54 bis criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'm going to have to ask you to come to a conclusion because of the hour and a half being up and the interpreters needing a break. Just give me one moment and let us confer for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me say what we have in mind and give the parties a few minutes to comment on it. What we have in mind, Mr. Djeric, is this: That we have here this priority list, and it's a starting point and it concentrates the minds on particular areas. What we have in mind is to give you two months to respond to this priority list. You would do that by very briefly indicating with a box, as it were, at the end your answer over-broad, or whatever it is, archival, where it can be produced, producing it if you can, complying as much as you can, obviously, but indicating that or when you can comply with it. In that way, the Trial Chamber will have before it all the arguments. You will also have more time to comply. And also, we would invite the Prosecutor, at this stage, if they can be -- the Prosecution, if they can be more specific, to be more specific on any of these particular archives as they're referred to. Mr. Djeric, is there anything you would want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, did you say two months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes indeed, I think that two months is sufficient. I think we would be able to provide you with brief answers or with a similar list commenting on this paper in less than two months. Therefore, then we could see what are the response that have been completely out of the agenda and what remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a matter of practicality, if you could do it on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Putting another box on the end, that would be very helpful, to make it much easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we recognise that this is your priority, but it does give us a document to work on, which at least has the advantage of being a specific document. We recognise it's not all of them. But we are minded to give the government some more time to consider the matter and to comply as far as possible. And we would then have the issues clarified, as far as we're concerned. The purpose being, of course, that as much as can be done by cooperation should be done and only ultimately should orders be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour is inviting me to speak, I see Mr. Djeric may not have concluded what he wants to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think for the moment there's nothing he wants to add on that, as I understand it. Bearing in mind, I'm afraid, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, I'm grateful for the indication. Can I make this perhaps obvious point: Given the time limits on us, this may be the critical hearing for determining how much documentary material of a highly important nature we can get before you. I'm afraid that our -- and I have to say this. Our experience is that granting time, or the government obtaining time, is usually a preface to them getting more time from us. And although I'm grateful for the very constructive approach that Your Honour is taking by saying give time and produce these documents, which is I think what Your Honour is saying, Your Honour will have in mind that 219, outstanding since June of last year for simply no good reason, is the very documents we would be wanting to call to put through witnesses whom, if we are to meet either the present time scale or any extended time scale, are witnesses who we've got to start having within the next couple of weeks, three weeks. We can't -- we cannot afford any more time. Of course, we've asked, you can consider the position of time at the moment and I've said that it may be, in due course, I'll have to apply for more time, but we are running up against the time. And what's happened is that the government concerned has taken its time. And you know, I was going to make this point amongst the few that may be allowed to me in the time available. One of the questions is what is an archive? Now, it's true that in an early stage in 1991 when we were looking for complete archives -- not looking for, we approached the authorities absolutely on the basis that there might be discussions about the mechanism of having access to them, by discussion with archivists and things of that sort. It was never the suggestion we should have the whole archive, it was always a question of assessment, which is the route that had been pursued with such success with the other entities. And it got somewhere with the Ministry of Justice, but once the documents became as critical as these, it was simply silence, no provision, no suggestion that what we were asking for was archives until the response to this application. And it's only this application, and a public application, that's flushed out a new defence. And when I say What is an archive? and deal with the Chamber's suggestion that archives might in some way be non-available to us, take the SDC. Now, there weren't actually very many meetings of it, it may be, because the accused, if our case is right, exercised control in other ways, and he exercised control on the SDC. You take all the SDC documents and you put them into a container and you say, "This is an archive." We say the SDC did operate. Critical to our case is to see how it operated because its very operation was reflective of the accused's criminality and guilt, and the fact that those documents are not available to us is indicative of the fact that there is something to hide. The authorities say, "Ah, but that's an archive." And if I may say so, the Chamber's approach to that may be somewhat unhelpful because it will encourage the categorisation as archives of documents that were never archives at all. The whole VJ army. Yes, that record is an archive and would need a different approach. But the meetings of the SDC, not at all. For example, when Mr. Djeric was speaking of the over-broadness of request number 117, contained within 117, which was made as long ago as August of 2001, was the Rules of Procedure of the Supreme Defence Council. That's a two-page document. There are two versions, different dates. I think it's about a two-page document which has now been provided in 2003. Item 2 was minutes of some meetings between April 1992 and 5th of October 2000, and the stenographic recordings of those meetings. Those meetings will exist. They will reflect how that Supreme Defence Council operated, and they will be highly reflective of the truth that underlines our case against this accused. So that, A, when there were archives, we were entirely straightforward about the desirability of going through archivists and assessments. We never got beyond that, and we have never sought possession of or generalised access to archives. And the word has been used in this response as a way of defence. And Your Honour will have noticed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's why I made the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed Your Honour did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because there is, to my mind, a clear distinction between the point being made about physical access to archives on the one hand and the question of the acceptability of a request for documents or information which may be found in something that is called an archive. That's an entirely different matter, and that has to be determined on the basis of the general criteria. So I don't think you should take it that the Chamber has accepted that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that. And it's very a helpful line, as it were, for us to have held because otherwise this would be probably used against us time and again as a ruling that barred us even making certain types of requests. Mr. Djeric says, you know, that they're anxious to see the solution to these terrible crimes, and so on. If I may say so, why are we here? We aren't here to burden ourselves with more material than we want, believe us. We are here simply to try and get the best material to help you, and that material lies with the authorities. And we have done the best we can to focus our requests, to repeat them and to explain their necessity, and we respectfully suggest that our outstanding requests should be the subject of a positive order but that certainly, as an interim measure, the priority list should be ordered, but two months is a very long time for things that have been outstanding, and it may be that a staggered order would be appropriate, and that is that all of those, and in particular all of 219, which is so important for upcoming witnesses and which are all outstanding then now for nine months, effectively, that those should be ordered in a far shorter space of time to enable us to put them through the witnesses we hope to call. So that, Your Honour -- those are probably my prime points. I'll see Ms. Milenov has been picking up the various requests, as they've been referred to by Mr. Djeric. No. The fundamental point is -- about archives is it's been a proper approach by us -- oh, there was something I was going to tell you, inform you about. Again, this hasn't been challenged. We received a proposal last year. I've got to check with Mr. Djeric because I'm not really a diplomat and I don't know about these things. I don't believe there's any objection to my mentioning what proposals were made by the authorities for the production of archival material insofar as the Supreme Defence Council material may now be being said to be archival. I see not. The proposal was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session and then the matter is covered in that way. We must be coming to a conclusion too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let Mr. Djeric finish, but very briefly, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJERIC
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. So we are asking you to reject the application in respect of the requests for assistance contained in part 1 of the application, and these are those requests that explicitly relate to archives. We think that we can meet your suggested time frame for the provision of the -- of the information about the pending requests for assistance. And in respect to 219, we are certain that we could provide information in a quite short time. As regards just one more sentence. As regards the proposals that we made to the Prosecution, I'm not going to go to the details in respect to 219, I would just like to repeat that these were legitimate consultations between the government and the Prosecution, that there was no intention to withhold anything from the Chamber, and that the Prosecution, according to our proposal, would be able to review the documents before we ask for protective measures in respect to those documents that the Prosecution wishes to have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice. Five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am probably not going to be that long. I've dealt with the history of references to archives which were through requests for assessment by contact with archivists to reflect the procedures with other entities. Any order that's made would, in our respectful submission, be much assisted by an order that the government makes absolutely clear its position in relation to the consequences of the bombing. There are duties on the state to preserve and to keep copies of documents. It must have either a good or very, very good view of exactly what was there, what didn't have copies elsewhere, and what did have copies elsewhere that we haven't yet been able to track down by a specific request; and a full and detailed answer from them on that is what would be appropriate, in our respectful submission. It appears that 219 is more available than the two months would require. We would invite it to be ordered forthwith. We cannot believe that those documents, having been the subject -- having been such Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. obviously important documents, sought now for nine months, haven't already been found, located and waiting for determination as to whether they should be handed over. They should be handed over forthwith. Issues of national security may arise with this problem as with any other. They should be dealt with at court or possibly by preliminary motion to the Court on a case-by-case basis. We all know the Chamber will be sympathetic but it is not appropriate to muddle issues of national security with issues of holding back or providing documents of this kind. I certainly do not regard the government as an adversary. I regard them as a body having duties of compliance with this Court which I have to ensure they perform insofar as it's up to me to do so by request and, where request fails, by application to the Court. That is all I've done, and that's all I'll do with them as with any other body. And, Your Honour, I think that's probably all I desire to say. Can I just check one thing? No, there are various -- various detailed pieces of information coming to me about matters that have been said, but I'm not sure that I'm in a position in the time available to summarise them. Can you just give me one moment, though? Your Honour, for the avoidance of any doubt or to avoid any confusion, there were requests about archives, that's the archives of the Yugoslav army, these are all back in 2001 and were at the time of the requests for meetings to get on with archivists and see what could be done. And as to the earlier assertion by Mr. Djeric that following the meeting that I was at in November of last year, there's been nothing but requests since then, that simply, as I understand it, isn't true. There were follow-up meetings of Mrs. Tromp, and I think Mr. Patrick Treanor in Belgrade within a few weeks of that and many other negotiations of a like kind. I repeat the point: We are only here because the efforts to get these materials by consent and by negotiation when we know they exist have foundered. And we understand, as I'm sure the Chamber does, that this material is critical to the best resolution of this case. If I can just read one more e-mail I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we must get on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered the submissions. For reasons which have been advanced during the course of argument, at the moment we think that a final determination of this matter would be premature and that a more productive course would be to adjourn it to allow the government to respond to the priority list of documents produced by the Prosecution today within two months, to comply with the requests in it as far and as soon as possible or to indicate the ground of objection where it's taken to any request. Having received that response, the Trial Chamber will consider what action is necessary, if any, and whether a further hearing is necessary. The Court will rise and sit again 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 5.00 p.m.
